## Learning objectives {.unnumbered}

By the end of this session, students should be able to:

- define a \(P_1\) finite-element approximation space on a triangular mesh;
- construct linear nodal shape functions directly on a physical triangle;
- derive the elemental stiffness matrix and elemental load vector;
- explain how local element contributions are assembled into a global linear system;
- relate local support of the basis functions to matrix sparsity;
- impose homogeneous and non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions;
- understand the practical role of the reference element, affine mapping, gradient transformation, and numerical quadrature.

## Schedule {.unnumbered}

| Time | Topic |
|---:|---|
| 0–15 min | Triangular mesh and definition of \(V_h\) |
| 15–35 min | \(P_1\) shape functions on one physical triangle |
| 35–50 min | Elemental stiffness matrix and load vector |
| 50–60 min | Global basis functions and assembly |
| 60–70 min | Local support, sparsity, and Dirichlet conditions |
| 70–90 min | Technical block: reference element, mapping, and quadrature |

# Triangular mesh and finite-element space

Let

$$
\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2
$$

be approximated by a triangulation

$$
\mathcal{T}_h
=
\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_{N_e}\}.
$$

The domain is decomposed into non-overlapping triangles:

$$
\Omega_h
=
\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h} T.
$$

For linear triangular finite elements, we define

$$
\boxed{
V_h
=
\left\{
v_h\in C^0(\Omega_h):
v_h|_T\in\mathbb{P}_1(T)
\quad
\forall T\in\mathcal{T}_h
\right\}.
}
$$

Thus, a finite-element function is:

- continuous over the whole mesh;
- affine on each individual triangle.

The finite-element approximation is written

$$
u_h(x,y)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N_h}
U_i\phi_i(x,y),
$$

where the global nodal basis functions satisfy

$$
\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_j)
=
\delta_{ij}.
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
U_i=u_h(\mathbf{x}_i).
}
$$

The coefficients of the finite-element approximation are therefore the nodal values of the approximate solution.

# \(P_1\) shape functions on one physical triangle

Consider one triangle

$$
T
=
\operatorname{conv}
\{
\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3
\},
$$

with

$$
\mathbf{x}_a=(x_a,y_a),
\qquad a=1,2,3.
$$

Inside \(T\), the finite-element solution is affine. If the three local vertices correspond to global nodes \(i_1,i_2,i_3\),

$$
u_h|_T(x,y)
=
U_{i_1}N_1(x,y)
+
U_{i_2}N_2(x,y)
+
U_{i_3}N_3(x,y).
$$

The local shape functions are affine:

$$
N_a(x,y)
=
a_a+b_a x+c_a y,
$$

and satisfy the nodal interpolation conditions

$$
\boxed{
N_a(\mathbf{x}_b)=\delta_{ab},
\qquad a,b=1,2,3.
}
$$

For example,

$$
N_1(\mathbf{x}_1)=1,
\qquad
N_1(\mathbf{x}_2)=N_1(\mathbf{x}_3)=0,
$$

and similarly for \(N_2\) and \(N_3\).

## Explicit construction

For each shape function

$$
N_a(x,y)=a_a+b_a x+c_a y,
$$

the coefficients are obtained from

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & y_1\\
1 & x_2 & y_2\\
1 & x_3 & y_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_a\\
b_a\\
c_a
\end{pmatrix}
=
\mathbf e_a,
$$

where \(\mathbf e_a\) is the \(a\)-th vector of the canonical basis of \(\mathbb R^3\).

Because the shape functions are affine,

$$
\boxed{
\nabla N_a
=
\begin{pmatrix}
b_a\\
c_a
\end{pmatrix}
}
$$

is constant over the triangle.

This property makes the \(P_1\) Poisson element particularly simple.

# Elemental stiffness matrix

For the Poisson problem,

$$
-\Delta u=f,
$$

the weak form contains the bilinear form

$$
a(u,v)
=
\int_\Omega
\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,d\Omega.
$$

On one triangle \(T\), the elemental stiffness matrix is defined by

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ab}
=
\int_T
\nabla N_a\cdot\nabla N_b\,d\Omega,
\qquad a,b=1,2,3.
}
$$

Since the gradients of the \(P_1\) shape functions are constant on \(T\),

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ab}
=
|T|\,
\nabla N_a\cdot\nabla N_b.
}
$$

The full elemental matrix is

$$
K^{(T)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
K^{(T)}_{11} & K^{(T)}_{12} & K^{(T)}_{13}\\
K^{(T)}_{21} & K^{(T)}_{22} & K^{(T)}_{23}\\
K^{(T)}_{31} & K^{(T)}_{32} & K^{(T)}_{33}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

# Elemental load vector

The right-hand side of the weak formulation is

$$
\ell(v)
=
\int_\Omega f v\,d\Omega.
$$

On one triangle,

$$
\boxed{
F_a^{(T)}
=
\int_T fN_a\,d\Omega,
\qquad a=1,2,3.
}
$$

Thus,

$$
F^{(T)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
F_1^{(T)}\\
F_2^{(T)}\\
F_3^{(T)}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For constant \(f\),

$$
\int_T N_a\,d\Omega
=
\frac{|T|}{3},
$$

and therefore

$$
\boxed{
F^{(T)}
=
\frac{f|T|}{3}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

For a general \(f(x,y)\), the integral is usually evaluated numerically.

> **FEM localizes both approximation and integration.**

# From local to global basis functions

A global nodal basis function \(\phi_i\) is obtained by joining the local shape functions associated with node \(i\) over all triangles containing that node.

Thus,

$$
\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_j)=\delta_{ij},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{supp}\phi_i
=
\bigcup
\left\{
T\in\mathcal{T}_h:
\mathbf{x}_i\in T
\right\}.
$$

The support of \(\phi_i\) is therefore local.

The global approximation is

$$
u_h
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N_h}
U_i\phi_i.
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-gmsh-mesh
#| fig-cap: "Coarse triangular mesh of a square domain containing a circular hole."
#| echo: true

import gmsh
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.tri as mtri

gmsh.initialize()
gmsh.model.add("square_with_hole")

# Geometry
L = 1.0
R = 0.18

square = gmsh.model.occ.addRectangle(0, 0, 0, L, L)
hole = gmsh.model.occ.addDisk(0.5, 0.5, 0, R, R)
gmsh.model.occ.cut([(2, square)], [(2, hole)])
gmsh.model.occ.synchronize()

# Deliberately coarse mesh for visualization
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMin", 0.16)
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMax", 0.22)
gmsh.model.mesh.generate(2)

# Extract nodes
node_tags, node_coords, _ = gmsh.model.mesh.getNodes()
coords = node_coords.reshape(-1, 3)
x = coords[:, 0]
y = coords[:, 1]

tag_to_index = {
    tag: i for i, tag in enumerate(node_tags)
}

# Extract 3-node triangles
element_types, _, element_nodes = gmsh.model.mesh.getElements(dim=2)

triangles = None

for element_type, nodes in zip(element_types, element_nodes):
    if element_type == 2:  # Gmsh type 2 = 3-node linear triangle
        nodes = nodes.reshape(-1, 3)
        triangles = np.array([
            [tag_to_index[tag] for tag in tri]
            for tri in nodes
        ])
        break

gmsh.finalize()

mesh = mtri.Triangulation(x, y, triangles)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
plt.triplot(mesh, linewidth=0.8)
plt.plot(x, y, ".", markersize=3)
plt.xlabel("$x$")
plt.ylabel("$y$")
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
```

The following figure selects one triangle and displays the three **global**
basis functions associated with its three vertices.

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-global-basis
#| fig-cap: "Three global $P_1$ basis functions associated with the vertices of one triangle."
#| echo: true

# Select a triangle whose centroid is close to this point
target_point = np.array([0.25, 0.50])

centroids_x = x[triangles].mean(axis=1)
centroids_y = y[triangles].mean(axis=1)

triangle_id = np.argmin(
    (centroids_x - target_point[0])**2
    + (centroids_y - target_point[1])**2
)

selected_nodes = triangles[triangle_id]

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 4.5))

for a, node in enumerate(selected_nodes):
    phi = np.zeros(len(x))
    phi[node] = 1.0

    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, a + 1, projection="3d")

    ax.plot_trisurf(
        mesh,
        phi,
        edgecolor="black",
        linewidth=0.5,
        alpha=0.9
    )

    ax.scatter([x[node]], [y[node]], [1.0], s=50)

    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
    ax.set_zlabel(r"$\phi_i$")
    ax.set_zlim(0, 1.05)
    ax.set_title(rf"Global basis function $\phi_{{i_{a+1}}}$")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Assembly of the global system

Suppose the local nodes

$$
1,\qquad 2,\qquad 3
$$

of one triangle correspond to the global nodes

$$
5,\qquad 12,\qquad 8.
$$

Then the elemental stiffness matrix is assembled by adding its entries to the corresponding entries of the global matrix:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
K_{5,5} & K_{5,12} & K_{5,8}\\
K_{12,5} & K_{12,12} & K_{12,8}\\
K_{8,5} & K_{8,12} & K_{8,8}
\end{pmatrix}
\; += \;
\begin{pmatrix}
K^{(T)}_{11} & K^{(T)}_{12} & K^{(T)}_{13}\\
K^{(T)}_{21} & K^{(T)}_{22} & K^{(T)}_{23}\\
K^{(T)}_{31} & K^{(T)}_{32} & K^{(T)}_{33}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
F_5\\
F_{12}\\
F_8
\end{pmatrix}
\; += \;
\begin{pmatrix}
F^{(T)}_1\\
F^{(T)}_2\\
F^{(T)}_3
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

After assembling all triangles,

$$
\boxed{KU=F.}
$$

# Local support and sparsity

The global stiffness entries are

$$
K_{ij}
=
\int_\Omega
\nabla\phi_i\cdot\nabla\phi_j\,d\Omega.
$$

If two nodal basis functions do not overlap,

$$
\operatorname{supp}\phi_i
\cap
\operatorname{supp}\phi_j
=
\varnothing,
$$

then

$$
K_{ij}=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{local support}
\Longrightarrow
\text{sparse global matrix}.
}
$$

Only nodes that belong to at least one common element can interact directly through the stiffness matrix.

# Dirichlet boundary conditions

## Homogeneous Dirichlet conditions

For

$$
u=0
\qquad
\text{on }\Gamma_D,
$$

the coefficients associated with Dirichlet nodes are prescribed:

$$
\boxed{
U_i=0
\qquad
\text{for all nodes }i\text{ on }\Gamma_D.
}
$$

The remaining degrees of freedom are unknown.

## Non-homogeneous Dirichlet conditions

Suppose instead that

$$
u=g
\qquad
\text{on }\Gamma_D.
$$

Split the degrees of freedom into

- \(U_f\): unknown (free) degrees of freedom;
- \(U_D\): prescribed Dirichlet degrees of freedom.

After grouping the corresponding rows and columns, write

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
K_{ff} & K_{fD}\\
K_{Df} & K_{DD}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
U_f\\
U_D
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
F_f\\
F_D
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The Dirichlet values are known:

$$
U_D=g_D.
$$

Substituting them into the equations corresponding to the unknown degrees of freedom gives

$$
K_{ff}U_f+K_{fD}g_D=F_f,
$$

hence

$$
\boxed{
K_{ff}U_f
=
F_f-K_{fD}g_D.
}
$$

The term \(-K_{fD}g_D\) is the algebraic lifting of the non-homogeneous Dirichlet data.

After solving for \(U_f\), the complete vector is reconstructed as

$$
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
U_f\\
g_D
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

# Technical block — reference element, mapping, and quadrature

The previous derivation was carried out directly on a physical triangle. This is sufficient to understand the finite-element construction.

In practical finite-element software, however, element integrals are evaluated systematically by mapping every physical triangle to the same reference triangle.

## Reference triangle

Define

$$
\widehat T
=
\left\{
(\xi,\eta):
\xi\ge0,\;
\eta\ge0,\;
\xi+\eta\le1
\right\}.
$$

Its vertices are

$$
(0,0),
\qquad
(1,0),
\qquad
(0,1).
$$

The \(P_1\) shape functions on the reference triangle are

$$
\widehat N_1=1-\xi-\eta,
\qquad
\widehat N_2=\xi,
\qquad
\widehat N_3=\eta.
$$

## Affine mapping

A physical triangle \(T\), with vertices
\(\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2,\mathbf x_3\), is obtained from \(\widehat T\) through

$$
\mathbf x(\xi,\eta)
=
\mathbf x_1
+
\xi(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1)
+
\eta(\mathbf x_3-\mathbf x_1).
$$

Its Jacobian is

$$
J
=
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(\xi,\eta)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_2-x_1 & x_3-x_1\\
y_2-y_1 & y_3-y_1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The area element transforms as

$$
\boxed{
d\Omega
=
|\det J|\,d\xi\,d\eta.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\int_T g(x,y)\,d\Omega
=
\int_{\widehat T}
g(\mathbf x(\xi,\eta))
|\det J|
\,d\xi\,d\eta.
}
$$

## Transformation of gradients

If

$$
N_a(x,y)
=
\widehat N_a(\xi,\eta),
$$

the chain rule gives

$$
\nabla_{\xi}\widehat N_a
=
J^T\nabla_x N_a.
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\nabla_x N_a
=
J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\widehat N_a.
}
$$

For an affine \(P_1\) triangle, \(J\) is constant over the element.

## Numerical quadrature on the reference triangle

An integral over the reference triangle is approximated by a sum over quadrature points:

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\widehat T}
g(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q\,g(\xi_q,\eta_q).
}
$$

Combining quadrature with the affine mapping gives

$$
\boxed{
\int_T g(x,y)\,d\Omega
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q\,
g(\mathbf x_q)\,
|\det J_q|,
}
$$

where

$$
\mathbf x_q
=
\mathbf x(\xi_q,\eta_q).
$$

For an affine triangle, \(J_q=J\) at every quadrature point.

### Poisson stiffness matrix in practice

For

$$
K^{(T)}_{ab}
=
\int_T
\nabla N_a\cdot\nabla N_b\,d\Omega,
$$

the practical quadrature formula is

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ab}
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q
\left(
J_q^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\widehat N_a(\xi_q,\eta_q)
\right)
\cdot
\left(
J_q^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\widehat N_b(\xi_q,\eta_q)
\right)
|\det J_q|.
}
$$

Similarly, the elemental load vector is computed as

$$
\boxed{
F_a^{(T)}
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q\,
f(\mathbf x_q)\,
\widehat N_a(\xi_q,\eta_q)\,
|\det J_q|.
}
$$

For the simplest one-point quadrature rule on \(\widehat T\),

$$
(\xi_1,\eta_1)
=
\left(
\frac13,\frac13
\right),
\qquad
w_1=\frac12.
$$

Thus,

$$
\int_{\widehat T}
g(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta
\approx
\frac12
g\left(\frac13,\frac13\right).
$$

This rule is exact for affine functions. In particular, it is exact for the
\(P_1\) stiffness integrand, which is constant on an affine triangle.

# Practical finite-element algorithm

For the Poisson problem, a basic finite-element code follows this sequence:

1. Generate a triangular mesh.
2. Define the nodal degrees of freedom.
3. For each triangle \(T\):
   - identify its global node numbers;
   - compute \(K^{(T)}\);
   - compute \(F^{(T)}\);
   - add these contributions to the global \(K\) and \(F\).
4. Impose Dirichlet boundary conditions.
5. Solve the reduced linear system.
6. Reconstruct

   $$
   u_h(x,y)
   =
   \sum_i U_i\phi_i(x,y).
   $$

The central computational structure is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\text{mesh}
\rightarrow
\text{local approximation}
\rightarrow
\text{element integrals}
\rightarrow
\text{assembly}
\rightarrow
\text{sparse global system}.
}
$$

Useful topics for understanding practical finite-element implementations in more detail include:

- Gaussian quadrature on triangles;
- higher-order elements;
